title: Jeremiah 20:7–13
context: Jeremiah speaks to the LORD in one of his most intense confessions. He says the LORD has persuaded him and prevailed, that he has become a laughingstock, and that the word of the LORD burns in him like fire when he tries to hold it in. Surrounded by whispers of Terror on every side, he nevertheless confesses that the LORD is with him like a mighty warrior, asks to see God’s vengeance, and breaks into praise. The sense of the word rendered persuaded is debated, and the notes give the readings with care.

verses.text: LORD, you have persuaded me, and I was persuaded. You are stronger than I, and have prevailed. I have become a laughingstock all day. Everyone mocks me.
verses.arminianNotes: LORD, you have persuaded me, and I was persuaded. Arminian readers note that the word rendered persuaded is rendered deceived or enticed in other translations, and some read it as Jeremiah’s bold complaint that the LORD overpowered him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the range of readings: God’s irresistible call, Jeremiah’s feeling of being misled about the cost, or both. The same verb appears in 20:10, where enemies hope Jeremiah will be persuaded.

verses.text: For as often as I speak, I cry out; I cry, “Violence and destruction!” because the LORD’s word has been made a reproach to me, and a derision, all day.
verses.arminianNotes: For as often as I speak, I cry out; Arminian readers see the prophet bearing the weight of a message that brings him only mockery.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note his words, the LORD’s word has been made a reproach to me, and a derision, all day. Faithfulness to God’s word costs Jeremiah his standing among his people.

verses.text: If I say that I will not make mention of him, or speak any more in his name, then there is in my heart as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones. I am weary with holding it in. I can’t.
verses.arminianNotes: If I say that I will not make mention of him, or speak any more in his name, Arminian readers see a real temptation to quit, and an inward compulsion that keeps Jeremiah speaking.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the image of a burning fire shut up in my bones. The word of God holds the prophet so powerfully that silence becomes unbearable.

verses.text: For I have heard the defaming of many: “Terror on every side! Denounce, and we will denounce him!” say all my familiar friends, those who watch for my fall. “Perhaps he will be persuaded, and we will prevail against him, and we will take our revenge on him.”
verses.arminianNotes: For I have heard the defaming of many: Arminian readers see Jeremiah surrounded by mockers and even by those who once were close, now watching for his fall.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the cry Terror on every side seems to echo the name given to Pashhur. The plotters hope that Jeremiah will be persuaded, using the same word as 20:7.

verses.text: But the LORD is with me as an awesome mighty one. Therefore my persecutors will stumble, and they won’t prevail. They will be utterly disappointed because they have not dealt wisely, even with an everlasting dishonor which will never be forgotten.
verses.arminianNotes: But the LORD is with me as an awesome mighty one. Arminian readers see a turn from complaint to confidence, as Jeremiah remembers the LORD’s promise to be with him (1:8).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the warrior image and the assurance that persecutors will stumble. The faith that surfaces here does not cancel the lament but stands within it.

verses.text: But the LORD of Armies, who tests the righteous, who sees the heart and the mind, let me see your vengeance on them, for I have revealed my cause to you.
verses.arminianNotes: But the LORD of Armies, who tests the righteous, who sees the heart and the mind, Arminian readers note that the verse closely resembles Jeremiah 11:20, where the prophet also commits his cause to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Jeremiah leaving vengeance with God, who sees the heart. The plea let me see your vengeance on them is a request, not a resolve to act himself.

verses.text: Sing to the LORD! Praise the LORD, for he has delivered the soul of the needy from the hand of evildoers.
verses.arminianNotes: Sing to the LORD! Praise the LORD, Arminian readers see sudden praise breaking into the lament, a reminder that faith and anguish can coexist in a single prayer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the needy are delivered from the hand of evildoers. The praise anticipates deliverance as certain, even while the danger and the mockery still remain.
